North America
United States of America
As sovereign, vibrant democracies, India and the
United States of America (USA) share a deep belief in
freedom, the rule of law, human rights, and pluralism.
The India–US Comprehensive Global Strategic
Partnership reflects a strong commitment to these
shared values and to future-oriented cooperation. The
partnership has benefited from enduring bipartisan
support in both countries, underscoring its strategic
significance and the broad-based public goodwill it
enjoys.
Regular leadership-level engagements have provided
continuity and strategic guidance, including the visit
of Prime Minister to Washington, D.C. in February
2025. Prime Minister was among the first global
leaders to hold a bilateral meeting with President
Donald J. Trump, underscoring the priority attached
to this relationship at the highest levels. Subsequent
ministerial and official interactions have continued to
reinforce shared priorities and advance cooperation
across sectors.
Prime Minister and President of the United States of America
US Donald J. Trump addressed a press conference at the White
House in Washington D.C., February 2025.
Today, the India-US partnership is anchored in more
than fifty dialogue mechanisms spanning across
diverse domains including foreign policy, defence,
trade, finance, energy, health, education, and space.
These institutionalised engagements—complemented

by active exchanges among think-tank communities
on both sides and regular visits by Members of the
US Congress and their staff—have ensured sustained
cooperation and steady progress across sectors
critical to national development and global stability,
while remaining responsive to evolving challenges
and emerging opportunities.
Defence and security cooperation has advanced
significantly, with a focus on co-production, co-
development, industrial partnerships, and increasingly
sophisticated joint military exercises. The shared
commitment to strategic technology collaboration
found expression in the TRUST (Transforming the
Relationship Utilizing Strategic Technology) initiative,
seeking to unlock new opportunities for co-innovation
and resilient supply chains. Both sides are also
negotiating the first tranche of a mutually beneficial,
multi-sector Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA), aimed
at deepening economic integration and facilitating
balanced, job-creating growth.
People-to-people ties continue to constitute a vital
pillar of the partnership. The Indian diaspora in the
United States, along with expanding linkages in
education, innovation, science and technology, and
culture, provides a dynamic and resilient foundation
for bilateral cooperation. These human connections
further enrich the strategic partnership by fostering
trust, familiarity, and enduring friendship between the
two societies.
High-Level Interactions
At the invitation of US President Donald J. Trump,
the Prime Minister visited Washington, D.C. on 12–
13 February for an Official Working Visit. This was
the Prime Minister’s first visit to the US, following
President Trump’s inauguration for a second term.
During the visit, the two leaders jointly launched
the US–India COMPACT (Catalysing Opportunities
for Military Partnership, Accelerated Commerce &
Technology) for the 21st Century, aimed at driving
transformative collaboration across key pillars of
bilateral cooperation, including Defence, Trade
and Investment, Energy Security, Technology and
Innovation, Multilateral Cooperation, and People-to-
People ties.
The Prime Minister also held meetings with the then
National Security Advisor Michael Waltz, Director of
National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, the then Head of
the Department of Government Efficiency and CEO of
Tesla Elon Musk and Vivek Ramaswamy.
The Prime Minister and President Trump held a
telephonic conversation on 22 April, during which
President Trump strongly condemned the terror attack
in Jammu & Kashmir and conveyed his condolences
and full support to India in bringing the perpetrators
to justice. The two leaders also held subsequent
telephone conversations on 18 June, 16 September,
9 October, 22 October and 11 December and have
remained in regular contact through public and private
communications, including via social media.
Prime Minister met US Vice President J.D. Vance on 11
February, on the sidelines of the Artificial Intelligence
(AI) Action Summit in France. Both sides held an
initial exchange of views on emerging technology
cooperation.
Vice President Vance paid an Official Visit to India
on 21–24 April, accompanied by Second Lady Usha
Vance, their children, and senior members of the US
Administration. This was Vice President Vance’s first
visit to India. The Prime Minister hosted the Vice
President at his residence, where they reviewed
progress across key areas of bilateral cooperation
and exchanged views on regional and global
developments of mutual interest. During the visit, Vice
President Vance also travelled to Jaipur and Agra.
Prime Minister met US Vice President J.D. Vance on the
sidelines of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Summit in
Paris, February 2025.

Commerce and Industry Minister (CIM) visited the US
on 3–6 March, 17–24 May, and 22–24 September for

The year also witnessed several high-level incoming
visits. US DNI Tulsi Gabbard visited India on 17–19
March to participate in the Raisina Dialogue. She
called on the Prime Minister and held bilateral
meetings with the Raksha Mantri, EAM, and National

EAM met US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth in Washington

US Ambassador-designate to India Sergio Gor and
Deputy Secretary for Management and Resources
Michael J. Rigas visited India on 9–14 October and
called on the Prime Minister, EAM, and the National

and Commerce Secretary.
Additionally, multiple US Congressional delegations
visited India during the year, including - a delegation
of Congressional Chiefs of Staff on 24–31 May,
bipartisan delegation of the House Permanent
Select Committee on Intelligence led by Reps. Brian
Fitzpatrick and Chrissy Houlahan on 20–21 August,
visit by Congressman Michael Baumgartner on 20–29
August and a five-member delegation led by Rep.
Ami Bera on 21–26 September.
Governors of Iowa and New Jersey - Kim Reynolds
and Phil Murphy, also visited India on 7–13 September
and 18–24 September, respectively.
Economic and Commercial Relations
As per US Census data, during January–December
2025, the two-way India–US merchandise trade
reached USD 149.43 billion, registering a 11.05%
growth over the corresponding period in the previous
year (2024). India’s merchandise exports to the US in
2025 stood at USD 103.82 billion, reflecting a growth
of 18.87%, while imports from the US reached USD
45.61 billion, an increase of 9.8% over the same
period last year, 2024.
The United States remains India’s third-largest source
of foreign direct investment (FDI), with cumulative
FDI inflows of USD 77.27 billion from April 2000 to
September 2025. During the period April–September
2025, FDI inflows from the United States amounted
to USD 6.6 billion, accounting for approximately 19
per cent of India’s total FDI equity inflows. As per
estimates over 2,000 US companies are currently
operating in India. According to the latest ‘Indian Roots,
American Soil’ report published by the Confederation
of Indian Industry (CII), cumulative Indian investment
in the United States stood at approximately USD 40
billion as of 2023, undertaken by around 160 Indian
companies.
US-origin Global Capability Centres (GCCs) constitute
the largest and most strategically significant segment
of India’s GCC ecosystem. Of the approximately
1,700–1,800 GCCs currently operating in India,
an estimated 55–60 percent are established by
US-headquartered
companies,
reflecting
deep
commercial integration and long-term confidence
in India’s talent and innovation ecosystem. In 2025
alone, US firms are estimated to have set up over
60 new GCCs across major Indian cities, with a
marked shift towards high-value activities. These
centres increasingly focus on advanced engineering,
product development, artificial intelligence (AI),
data analytics, cybersecurity, healthcare technology,
financial services, and global business transformation,
moving well beyond traditional back-office functions.

228
US GCCs have emerged as critical nodes in global
innovation networks, supporting core business
operations, driving R&D, and anchoring India’s role as
a trusted partner in global technology and services
value chains.
During the Prime Minister’s visit to Washington, D.C. in
February, the two leaders reaffirmed their commitment
to strengthening bilateral trade and economic
cooperation in a manner that advances fairness,
national security, resilience, and job creation in both
countries. The leaders agreed to set an ambitious new
target, ‘Mission 500’, to more than double bilateral
trade to USD 500 billion by 2030. Recognising that
achieving this shared ambition would require updated
and mutually beneficial trade arrangements, the two
sides announced the launch of negotiations for a multi-
sector Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA). Since then,
the two sides have engaged in intensive discussions
to finalise the initial tranche of the Agreement.
Despite substantive progress in negotiations on
31 July, the US imposed reciprocal tariffs on certain
goods exported by several countries, including
India, invoking national emergency authorities under
the International Emergency Economic Powers Act
(IEEPA). Subsequently, on 27 August an additional
25 per cent ad-valorem duty was imposed on select
Indian exports under IEEPA, citing India’s importation
of Russian oil. In parallel, the US also imposed
sector-specific tariffs under Section 232 of the Trade
Expansion Act on products including steel and
aluminium, copper, upholstered furniture and kitchen
cabinets, softwood, and automobiles.
At the same time, several categories of goods and
services - including crude oil and petroleum products,
pharmaceuticals, bullion, certain electronic items,
precious metals, critical minerals, resins and plastics,
agricultural products, and IT services—have not
been subject to these additional tariffs. Based on
2024 trade data, approximately USD 47.2 billion of
India’s merchandise exports to the United States, out
of a total of about USD 86.4 billion, fall within tariff-
affected categories.
Notwithstanding these developments, negotiations
towards a mutually beneficial BTA have continued.
The latest round of negotiations was held in
Washington, D.C. on 15–17 October. Subsequently,
US Deputy Trade Representative Rick Switzer led a
delegation to India on 10–11 December, during which
he met senior Government officials. Both sides remain
actively engaged in advancing the negotiations.
Minister of Finance spoke to Treasury Secretary Scott
Bessent over telephone in May and December to
discuss bilateral economic issues. Both sides agreed
to continue the Economic and Financial Partnership
Dialogue (EFP) at the Ministerial level.
In October, Secretary, Department of Economic Affairs
led India’s delegation for the Annual Fund Bank
meetings in Washington D.C. During the meeting she
held a bilateral meeting with the Under Secretary of
State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg.
Energy Cooperation
The United States is India’s sixth-largest energy
trade partner. India’s energy imports from the United
States—including crude oil, LNG, and petroleum
products—amounted to USD 10.37 billion during the
first ten months of 2025, representing a growth of
38 per cent compared to the corresponding period in
2024.
Under the India–US COMPACT framework, both
countries have committed to deepening the US–India
Energy Security Partnership, including cooperation
in oil, gas, and civil nuclear energy. Both sides
share a strong commitment to advancing peaceful
nuclear cooperation and associated research and
development activities. Strengthened science and
technology cooperation over the past several years has
benefitted both countries, as well as partner countries
worldwide. In line with this objective, on 15 January,
following an interagency review, the US Bureau of
Industry and Security (BIS) removed three Indian
entities - Indian Rare Earths Ltd. (IREL), Indira Gandhi
Atomic Research Centre (IGCAR), and Bhabha Atomic
Research Centre (BARC)—from the US ‘Entity List.’ BIS
stated that this decision supported US foreign policy
objectives by reducing barriers to advanced energy

cooperation, including joint research and development
and enhanced science and technology collaboration,
in pursuit of shared energy security goals.
During Prime Minister’s visit to Washington, D.C. in
February and interaction with President Trump, the two
leaders reiterated their commitment to fully realizing
the US–India 123 Civil Nuclear Agreement. They
agreed to advance plans for the construction of US-
designed nuclear reactors in India, supported by large-
scale localization and potential technology transfer.
Both sides also welcomed the Government of India’s
Budget announcement proposing amendments to the
Atomic Energy Act and the Civil Liability for Nuclear
Damage Act (CLNDA), aimed at facilitating greater
collaboration between Indian and U.S. industry in
nuclear reactor manufacturing and deployment. In the
same month, the United States reaffirmed its strong
support for India’s full membership in the International
Energy Agency (IEA).
EAM met US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright in
Washington, D.C. on 1 July, during which both sides
discussed a broad range of issues related to energy
cooperation of mutual interest.
On 19 February, Minister of Petroleum and Natural
Gas (MoPNG) held a telephonic discussion with his
counterpart Secretary, US Department of Energy
Chris Wright. Both sides reviewed the ongoing
energy cooperation between the two sides and
announced the India-US Energy Security Partnership
(ESP), envisaged as a comprehensive bilateral energy
cooperation framework covering all forms of energy.
India and the US also launched the Strategic Mineral
Recovery Initiative in February, aimed at recovering
and processing critical minerals—including lithium,
cobalt, and rare earth elements—from heavy
industries such as aluminium, coal mining, and oil
and gas. The inaugural meeting of the Expert Group
under this initiative was held virtually on 15 July. The
U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) is in the process of
preparing a roadmap to guide further engagement
under this initiative.
Regulatory cooperation also continued during the year.
The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) of India
and the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC)
held a bilateral technical meeting from 6–8 August
to exchange perspectives on regulatory frameworks,
safety standards, and licensing processes for advanced
reactors and Small Modular Reactors (SMRs).
Secretary, Ministry of Coal led a delegation to the U.S.
in August to explore possibilities for collaboration in
coal gasification. Both sides expressed strong interest
in advancing cooperation in this area and are working
towards the conclusion of an MoU on the subject.
Representatives from Coal India Limited, Bharat Coal
Gasification and Chemicals Limited, and NLC India
Limited were also part of the delegation.
The US welcomed the passage of the Sustainable
Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for
Transforming India (SHANTI) Bill 2025, by the Indian
Parliament on 18 December. The bill consolidates
laws governing the civil nuclear sector and enables
participation by private players. In a statement, the US
Embassy in New Delhi noted that it stands ready to
pursue joint innovation and research and development
in the energy sector.
Meanwhile, several private-sector civil nuclear
collaborations, including proposals related to SMRs,
remained under active consideration and made
progress. In 2025, the US Department of Energy
granted specific authorizations under ten CFR Part 810

Defence Cooperation
The India–US defence partnership remains one of the
most consequential pillars of the bilateral relationship.
Anchored in a robust framework of foundational
defence agreements, the partnership has expanded
to encompass ministerial-level dialogues, extensive
military-to-military
engagement,
acquisition
of
advanced defence platforms, information sharing, joint
exercises, co-production and technology cooperation,
as well as collaboration in emerging domains such as
space and AI. This growing cooperation has enhanced
interoperability across land, maritime, air, space, and
cyber domains, and has emerged as an important
contributor to stability in the Indo-Pacific region.
During the Prime Minister’s meeting with President
Trump in February, both leaders reaffirmed their
commitment to the dynamic defence partnership
spanning multiple domains. They announced plans to
sign a new ten-year Framework for the US–India Major
Defence Partnership in the 21st Century, and discussed
expansion of defence sales and co-production to
strengthen interoperability and defence industrial
cooperation. Both sides agreed to accelerate defence
technology cooperation across space, air defence,
missile, maritime, and undersea technologies. The
leaders also announced the Autonomous Systems
Industry Alliance (ASIA) initiative to scale industry
partnerships and production in the Indo-Pacific.
Both sides further announced their intent to review
respective arms-transfer regulations, including the
International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR).
Raksha Mantri and US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth
signed the new and ambitious ten-year Framework
for the US–India Major Defence Partnership in the 21st
Century (2025–35) on the sidelines of the ADMM+
Meeting in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.
EAM held a bilateral meeting with Secretary of
War Pete Hegseth on 1 July in Washington, D.C.
and discussed the strategic importance of India–US
defence ties. They welcomed the expanding bilateral
defence trade and deepening partnership in areas
such as Underwater Domain Awareness (UDA) and
autonomous systems.
Foreign Secretary visited Washington D.C. in May,
and held meetings with Deputy Secretary of Defence
Steve Feinberg and Under Secretary for Policy
Elbridge Colby. The discussions focused on co-
production and co-development initiatives, sustained
joint military exercises, logistics and information-
sharing frameworks, and enhancing interoperability
between the armed forces.
Chief of the Naval Staff undertook an official visit to
the United States on 12–17 November. During the
visit, he met Commander of the U.S. Indo-Pacific
Command (US INDOPACOM) Admiral Samuel Paparo;
Commander, U.S. Pacific Fleet Admiral Stephen
Koehler, and Commander, US Marine Forces Pacific
Lieutenant General James Glynn, to advance maritime
cooperation and discuss maritime security in the Indo-
Pacific region.
Additionally, the year witnessed multiple incoming
high-level interactions. US INDOPACOM Commander
Admiral Samuel Paparo visited India in March to
participate in the Raisina Dialogue 2025 and held
interactions with his counterparts and senior Indian
officials.
Director, Defence Innovation Unit (DIU) Douglas Beck,
and Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defence for South
and Southeast Asia Andrew Byers visited India in
April and met senior officials in the MEA and MoD, as
well as DRDO.
An introductory bilateral meeting took place in New
Delhi on 8 July between the defence officials of the two
sides regarding the Reciprocal Defence Procurement
Agreement. The U.S. delegation was led by Principal
Director of Defence Pricing and Contracting (DPC)
John Tengalia. The DPC is within the Office of the
Secretary of Defence (OSD).
The Indian Army received the full batch of six AH–
64E Apache attack helicopters from the US in two
tranches – tranche one in July, and the remaining three
helicopters in December.

231
US INDOPACOM Commander Admiral Samuel Paparo held a
bilateral meeting with Chief of Defence Staff of India on the
sidelines of Raisina Dialogue held in New Delhi, March 2025.
Institutional
dialogue
mechanisms
were
also
advanced. The bilateral 2+2 Intersessional Meeting,
led by senior officials from the MEA and MoD and
the U.S. Departments of State and Defence, was
held virtually on 25 August. Separately, a delegation
of officials from the Office of the Under Secretary
of War (OUSW), Space Policy, visited India on
23–27 September and held discussions regarding
cooperation in the defence–space domain.
In September, a delegation comprising officials from
the US Department of War and Boeing Company
visited India to hold negotiations regarding potential
procurement of six additional P–8I aircraft by India.
The Executive Steering Group (ESG) Meeting for the
Army was held in New Delhi in May, while the Navy
ESG Meeting was held in New Delhi in December. The
24th India–US Joint Technology Group (JTG) meeting,
co-chaired by the Office of the US Under Secretary
of Defence for Research and Engineering and DRDO,
was held in New Delhi on 30–31 October.
The 22nd India–US Military Cooperation Group (MCG)
meeting was held in Hawaii on 3–4 November. The
meeting was co-chaired by India’s Chief of Integrated
Defence Staff and Lieutenant General Joshua Rudd of
the US INDOPACOM.
During 2025, India and the US conducted several joint
defence exercises, both in bilateral and multilateral
formats. The Indian Navy participated in the US-led
multilateral anti-submarine warfare Exercise Sea
Dragon held in March in Guam. The fourth edition of
the tri-services Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster
Relief (HADR) amphibious Exercise Tiger Triumph was
held in April at Visakhapatnam. A two-day unmanned
systems Subject Matter Expert Exchange (SMEE)
Technology Event was held during the exercise for
the first time, to advance the ASIA initiative. The
first-ever independent Special Forces Exercise Tiger
Claw between the Indian Air Force and the United
States Air Force (USAF) was conducted in May–June
across various locations in North India. In September,
Exercise Yudh Abhyas was held in Alaska, USA, with
a significant increase in the scope and complexity of
the joint exercise. Exercise Malabar was conducted
at and off Guam in November, and Exercise Cope
India was held in November with Japan and Australia
participating as observers.
Defence trade and industrial collaboration recorded
significant progress. In July, the Indian Army received
the first batch of three AH–64E Apache attack
helicopters from the United States, with the final
batch delivered on 16 December. On 7 November,
Hindustan Aeronautics Limited signed a USD 1 billion
contract with GE Aerospace for 113 GE F404 engines,
in addition to 99 engines contracted earlier. On 19
November, the U.S. State Department approved two
defence sales to India valued at USD 92.8 million,
covering FGM-148 Javelin missiles and M982A1
Excalibur guided artillery projectiles. On 28 November,
agreements worth USD 946 million were signed
with the United States for maintenance and support
of the Indian Navy’s MH-60R Seahawk helicopter
fleet. On 4 December, the United States approved
the release of MAC sonobuoys, towed array systems,
seabed sensors, and other unmanned underwater
vehicle systems to India, further strengthening India’s
undersea warfare capabilities. On 8 December, Tata
Advanced Systems and Lockheed Martin announced
the commencement of a Defence Maintenance, Repair
and Overhaul facility in Bengaluru to support C-130J
Super Hercules aircraft. The construction of the C130J
MRO is expected to be finished by the end of 2026
and the facility will begin receiving C130J platforms
in early 2027.

Strategic Technology Cooperation
Science and technology cooperation has been a
cornerstone of the strategic partnership between the
world’s two largest democracies. On 5–6 January,
former US National Security Advisor Jake Sullivan,
visited India with a senior interagency delegation
to review progress under the India–U.S. Initiative on
Critical and Emerging Technologies (iCET), which has
since been recast as the TRUST (Transforming the
Relationship Utilizing Strategic Technology) initiative.
The review covered cooperation across artificial
intelligence, quantum computing, semiconductors,
telecommunications, defence, and space.
During the Prime Minister’s visit to the United States in
February, both sides formally announced the launch of
the U.S.–India TRUST initiative. TRUST aims to catalyse
collaboration among governments, industry, academia,
and research institutions to advance cooperation
in defence, artificial intelligence, semiconductors,
quantum technologies, biotechnology, energy, and
space, while promoting the use of trusted and verified
technology vendors and ensuring the protection of
sensitive technologies. During the visit, the leaders
also launched INDUS Innovation, a new innovation
bridge modelled on the INDUS-X platform to facilitate
partnerships among defence companies, investors,
and universities, and announced the Strategic Mineral
Recovery Initiative to recover and process critical
minerals—including lithium, cobalt, and rare earths—
from industrial sectors such as aluminium, coal mining,
and oil and gas.
An MoU between the US National Science Foundation
(NSF) and the Indian Anusandhan National Research
Foundation (ANRF) was signed and announced
during the Prime Minister’s visit to the United States
in February. This partnership builds on the ongoing
collaboration between the NSF and several Indian
science agencies to enable joint research in the areas
of semiconductors, connected vehicles, machine
learning,
next-generation
telecommunications,
intelligent transportation systems, and future bio-
manufacturing.
Further momentum to India-US strategic technology
cooperation was provided by the visit of the Foreign
Secretary and Deputy National Security Advisor to
Washington D.C. on 28–29 May focused on advancing
the TRUST initiative. Discussions also covered the
Indian Ocean Strategic Venture (IOSV), as well as
cooperation through I2U2 and the India–Middle
East–Europe Economic Corridor (IMEEC). In addition,
a Track 1.5 Dialogue under the Advanced Materials
R&D Forum was held virtually in August to support
collaboration in advanced materials and resilient
supply chains.
Engagements on digital and cyber issues continued
through high-level exchanges. A delegation led by
Indian and US armed forces participated in the fourth edition of the tri-services Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR)
amphibious Exercise Tiger Triumph held in Visakhapatnam, April 2025.

text:
The Americas
233
Senior Advisor at the Cyber and Digital Policy Bureau at
the US Department of State Alka Patel visited India on
8 September for discussions on artificial intelligence,
advanced materials, rare earths, and pharmaceuticals.
This was followed by Senior Bureau Official for the
Bureau of Cyberspace and Digital Policy Russell
C. Headlee’s visit to India on 10 December, which
focused on preparations for the upcoming AI Impact
Summit and broader issues related to cyberspace and
digital policy.
During 2025, US technology companies significantly
deepened their engagement with India’s artificial
intelligence (AI) ecosystem through large-scale
investments in digital infrastructure and sustained
commitments to talent development. Major US firms
announced multi-billion-dollar investments in AI, cloud
computing, and data centre infrastructure. Microsoft
announced an investment of USD 17.5 billion to
expand AI and cloud infrastructure, data centres, and
associated digital skilling initiatives in India; Amazon
committed over USD 35 billion by 2030 to strengthen
AI capabilities, digital infrastructure, exports, and
small business enablement; and Google unveiled a
USD 15 billion plan to establish a major AI hub and
gigawatt-scale data centre campus in Visakhapatnam.
Taken together, these commitments—amounting to
over USD 67 billion—underscore strong U.S. investor
confidence in India as a key destination for AI-driven
growth and digital transformation.
Leading US technology firms continued to expand
AI-related operations encompassing research and
development, cloud and compute infrastructure,
enterprise AI solutions, and platform support
functions. Notably, frontier AI companies such as
OpenAI initiated steps towards establishing a formal
office presence in India, while Anthropic advanced
plans to set up operations in Bengaluru, signaling
deeper engagement by the US' AI model developers
with the Indian ecosystem.
In parallel, US companies expanded investments in
AI training and workforce development, recognising
the importance of skills for sustainable AI adoption.
Microsoft scaled up nationwide AI skilling programmes,
while Amazon Web Services continued large-scale
cloud and AI training through initiatives such as
AWS Skill Builder, AWS Educate, and AWS re/Start.
Databricks announced an investment of over USD
250 million to support data and AI training through
the India Data + AI Academy, and Kyndryl expanded
AI-focused skilling programmes and innovation labs
in India. Collectively, these initiatives reinforced India’s
emergence as a global hub for AI infrastructure,
innovation, and talent.
In semiconductors, US companies continued to
play an important role in strengthening India’s
ecosystem, supported by incentives under the
India Semiconductor Mission and global supply-
chain diversification efforts. Engagements during
the year spanned assembly and testing, equipment
manufacturing, design, advanced packaging, and
skills development. Micron Technology advanced
implementation of its USD 2.75 billion Assembly,
Test, Marking and Packaging (ATMP) facility in Gujarat,
achieving key regulatory and operational milestones.
U.S. semiconductor equipment firms, including Lam
Research, expanded supply-chain localisation and
sourcing of critical components in India, while leading
design and technology companies such as AMD,
Qualcomm, and Intel further strengthened India-based
R&D and ecosystem partnerships. In this context, the
Tata Group and Intel announced a strategic alliance
to explore collaboration in hardware enablement
and semiconductor and systems manufacturing,
supporting India’s domestic semiconductor ecosystem
and the development of a geo-resilient electronics
and semiconductor supply chain. Collectively, these
developments underscored deepening India–U.S.
cooperation in critical and emerging technologies.
Space Cooperation
India and the United States share a long-standing
partnership in the civil space domain, encompassing
cooperation in Earth observation, satellite navigation,
space science, exploration, and commercial space
activities. During 2025, this cooperation witnessed
title: mea_annual_report

text:
ANNUAL REPORT | 2025
234
significant
milestones
across
scientific,
human
spaceflight, and commercial dimensions, reinforcing
space as a key pillar of the India–US Comprehensive
Global Strategic Partnership.
A major highlight of the year was the successful
launch of the NASA–ISRO Synthetic Aperture
Radar (NISAR) mission on 30 July from the Satish
Dhawan Space Centre, India. NISAR is a first-of-its-
kind joint microwave imaging satellite developed by
the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and
the National Aeronautics and Space Administration
(NASA) to provide high-resolution, all-weather data
for applications including disaster management,
climate change studies, agriculture, and ecosystem
monitoring. Under the mission, ISRO contributed
the S-band radar, spacecraft bus systems, the
GSLV launch vehicle, and is responsible for mission
operations, while NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory
provided the L-band radar, GPS receiver, solid-state
recorder, and high data-rate downlink system. The
satellite’s initial operational phase has been highly
satisfactory, and commissioning for the science phase
is currently underway.
Bilateral cooperation also deepened significantly in the
area of human spaceflight. An ISRO-nominated Indian
Gaganyaatri, Group Captain Shubhanshu Shukla,
participated in the Axiom-4 (Ax-4) commercial mission
to the International Space Station, a joint endeavour
involving ISRO, NASA, and U.S. commercial partners.
The mission was launched on 25 June and concluded
on 15 July, following an 18-day stay aboard the ISS,
during which scientific experiments relevant to India’s
human spaceflight programme were conducted.
In connection with the mission, the Secretary,
Department of Space, visited the NASA Kennedy
Space Center, Florida, and the NASA Johnson Space
Center, Houston, underscoring close institutional
coordination between ISRO and NASA.
In the area of space safety and mission assurance,
cooperation continued under the Hyper Velocity
Impact Test (HVIT) agreement between ISRO and
NASA. As part of this framework, ISRO officials
completed the first phase of Micro Meteoroidal and
Orbital Debris (MMOD) impact testing of Gaganyaan
crew module shields at NASA’s White Sands Test
Facility in October, contributing to enhanced safety
and reliability of India’s human spaceflight systems.
Commercial space cooperation also expanded during
the year, reflecting growing linkages between Indian
industry as well as US launch and satellite ecosystems.
Satellites developed by Indian private companies,
including a hyperspectral constellation from Pixxel,
as well as satellites from Dhruva Space and HEX20,
were launched aboard Falcon-9 launch vehicles
in the United States during the year. In a significant
reciprocal development, ISRO successfully launched
a next-generation U.S. communication satellite,
BlueBird Block-2, for AST SpaceMobile, using its
heaviest launch vehicle LVM3-M6 from Sriharikota on
24 December, highlighting India’s growing role as a
reliable launch service provider for global commercial
customers.
High-level exchanges further reinforced bilateral
engagement in the space sector. A delegation led
by Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs U.S.
Department of State Allison Hooker visited ISRO
Headquarters in Bengaluru on 10 December, where
discussions covered ongoing and future areas of
cooperation in civil and commercial space. During
the visit, the U.S. side also highlighted progress on
NASA’s Artemis-II lunar human spaceflight mission,
targeted for launch in early 2026.
Overall, during 2025, India–US space cooperation
registered tangible progress across joint satellite
missions, human spaceflight, space safety, and
commercial launches, supported by strong institutional
linkages and high-level political engagement. These
developments underscored the growing depth,
maturity, and strategic significance of India–U.S.
collaboration in the peaceful exploration and use of
outer space.

Counter-Narcotics Cooperation
Recognising the transnational nature of the threat
of narcotics trafficking, India–U.S. cooperation in
this domain has steadily deepened over the past
three decades and is anchored in the 1990 Bilateral
Agreement on Mutual Cooperation, the 1994
Memorandum of Understanding, and, more recently,
the 2024 MoU on the Drug Policy Framework. The
creation of the India–U.S. Counter-Narcotics Working
Group (CNWG) during President Trump’s visit to India
in 2020 has further institutionalised this partnership
and provided a structured mechanism for sustained
engagement.
At the fifth CNWG meeting held in October 2024,
a strengthened two-tier structure was adopted,
comprising an Executive Working Group and three
thematic pillars focused on disrupting trafficking
networks, advancing public health cooperation, and
securing pharmaceutical supply chains.
Operational
and
capacity-building
cooperation
between the two countries has yielded tangible
results. Over the period 2021–2025, Indian and
U.S. enforcement agencies conducted 38 controlled
delivery operations and exchanged over 180
actionable intelligence inputs, leading to significant
seizures of narcotics, precursor chemicals, and
psychotropic substances, and the disruption of
courier networks, parcel-based trafficking, and online
vendors. In July, Indian agencies led by the Narcotics
Control Bureau dismantled a major international drug
cartel under Operation MED MAX through multi-
agency cooperation, triggering coordinated actions
in the United States and Australia against a network
operating across four continents and more than ten
countries.
Capacity-building cooperation, including training and
workshops on clandestine laboratories, emerging
synthetic drugs, and forensic techniques—with
support from the US Drug Enforcement Administration,
Homeland Security Investigations, and the Department
of Justice—has further deepened collaboration
and enhanced enforcement capabilities. High-level
engagement continued with the visit of the U.S. Office
of National Drug Control Policy Senior Advisor Debbie
Seguin to India on 10–14 August. Together, these
efforts underscore the depth of trust, operational
coordination, and shared commitment underpinning
India–US cooperation in addressing evolving narcotics
threats while safeguarding legitimate pharmaceutical
and industrial supply chains.
Counter Terrorism and Security
Cooperation
Counterterrorism cooperation remains a central pillar
of the India–US Strategic Partnership, encompassing
information exchange, capacity building, operational
collaboration, mutual legal assistance (including
extradition), and regular consultations under the India–
US Joint Working Group on Counterterrorism (JWG-
CT). Both sides also cooperate closely on terrorist
designations through the bilateral Designations
Dialogue, as well as in multilateral and international
fora including the United Nations and the Financial
Action Task Force (FATF).
During the Prime Minister’s visit to Washington, D.C. in
February, the two leaders reaffirmed their commitment
to jointly counter terrorist threats posed by groups
including Al-Qaeda, ISIS, Jaish-e-Mohammad, and
Lashkar-e-Tayyiba, with the objective of preventing
attacks of the kind witnessed during the 26/11 Mumbai
terrorist attacks. The India–U.S. Joint Statement of
13 February called upon Pakistan to ensure that its
territory is not used for launching cross-border terrorist
attacks. On the same day, President Donald Trump
announced that his Administration had approved the
extradition of Tahawwur Rana, one of the conspirators
in the 2008 Mumbai attacks. Tahawwur Rana was
subsequently extradited to India on 9 April, marking
a significant milestone in bilateral counterterrorism
cooperation.
The United States also took the lead in mobilising
international support following the terrorist attack in
Pahalgam on 22 April, including through a UN Security
Council Press Statement condemning the attack. The
Quad Foreign Ministers’ Joint Statement of 1 July,
title: mea_annual_report

ANNUAL REPORT | 2025

issued in Washington, D.C., similarly condemned
the attack in the strongest terms and called for the
perpetrators, organisers, and financiers to be brought
to justice without delay. Further underscoring this
commitment, on 18 July, the US Department of State
designated The Resistance Front (TRF)—a Lashkar-
e-Tayyiba front and proxy—as a Foreign Terrorist
Organization (FTO) and a Specially Designated Global
Terrorist (SDGT). TRF had claimed responsibility for
the Pahalgam attack, which killed 26 civilians. In
announcing the designation, US Secretary of State
Marco Rubio stated that the action reflected the
Administration’s commitment to countering terrorism
and enforcing justice for the victims.
Institutional engagement continued with the 21st
meeting of the India–US Joint Working Group on
Counterterrorism and the seventh Designations
Dialogue, held on 3 December in New Delhi. The
Indian delegation was led by Joint Secretary (Counter
Terrorism), Ministry of External Affairs, while the
US side was led by Senior Bureau Official, Bureau
of Counterterrorism, U.S. Department of State
Monica Jacobsen. The discussions reviewed threat
assessments, operational cooperation, and progress
on designations and legal cooperation.
Both
sides
also
intensified
law
enforcement
cooperation to take decisive action against illegal
immigration networks, organised crime syndicates
(including narco-terrorist groups), and human and
arms trafficking networks, which pose threats to public
safety, diplomatic security, and national sovereignty.
This shared resolve was reiterated in discussions
on mobility and security cooperation, emphasising
firm action against criminal facilitators alongside the
need to enable safe, secure, and orderly movement
of people. Between 1 January and 31 December, a
total of 3,567 Indian nationals were repatriated to
India under US deportation procedures. The Ministry
of External Affairs remained in close coordination
with US authorities to ensure that deportations were
conducted in a humane manner, with due regard for the
dignity and well-being of the individuals concerned.
In addition, on 17 January, India and the United States
signed an MoU in Washington, D.C. to enhance
cooperation in cybercrime investigations. The MoU
provides a framework for closer collaboration and
specialised training in cyber threat intelligence and
digital forensics, strengthening the capacity of law
enforcement agencies in both countries to investigate
and prosecute cyber-enabled criminal activity.
Education, Culture and People-to-People
Ties
Indian diaspora in the US amounts to around 5.4
million. Indian-origin professionals, entrepreneurs,
and students have emerged as central contributors
to
America’s
innovation
economy
and
global
competitiveness. They are driving research, value
creation, and technological breakthroughs across
Silicon Valley, cutting-edge defence laboratories,
and leading university research centers. Today,
Indian-origin CEOs head some of the United States’
most influential and high-value companies. Their
leadership directly strengthens economic growth,
global competitiveness, shareholder value, and high-
quality job creation in the American economy. The
achievements of the Indian-American represent not
only individual success stories, but also a living bridge
of trust, talent, and shared aspirations between our
two nations.
Eight new Indian Consular Application Centers (ICAC)
across the United States of America were inaugurated
on 1 August. The new ICACs have been opened in
Raleigh, Orlando, San Jose, Dallas, Detroit, Columbus,
Edison, and Boston. This expansion makes consular
services more accessible to Indian and American
citizens in the United States.
During Prime Minister’s visit to the U.S. in February,
both leaders recognized that the talent flow and
movement of students, researchers and employees,
has mutually benefitted both countries.
Indian professionals have made sustained contributions
to innovation, economic growth, and technological
advancement in the United States, while also acquiring

237
expertise and experience that strengthens India’s own
innovation and entrepreneurial ecosystem through
return, collaboration, and cross-border engagement.
The Ministry continues to engage with US authorities
to underscore the shared benefits of people-to-people
ties and skilled mobility, and to advocate for policies
that preserve and sustain this productive partnership
in the long-term interest of both countries.
Education partnership is an important pillar of India-
US ties with strong linkages and history of higher
education collaborations. Indian students annually
contribute in excess of USD 10 billion to the U.S.
economy. In December, there were about 3,53,737
Indian students in the U.S., 80% of whom are pursuing
graduate (masters) programs. During Prime Minister’s
visit to US, both leaders resolved to strengthen
collaborations between the higher education including
through setting up of offshore campuses of premier
educational institutions of the US in India. A Letter of
Intent was issued to Illinois Institute of Technology
to set-up Campus in Mumbai, and several other
collaborations are being explored.
On the culture front, on 28 July, the US published a
Designated List of Archaeological and Ethnological
Material of India which amends the US Customs
and Border Protection (CBP) regulations to reflect
the imposition of import restrictions on certain
archaeological
and
ethnological
material
from
India. As per the rule, effective from 28 July 2025
to 26 July 2029, unless extended, the importation
of these materials to the USA is restricted unless
they are accompanied by documentation certifying
that they left India legally and are not in violation of
India’s export laws. The import restrictions apply on
certain categories of archaeological material from
India, ranging in date from approximately 1.7 million
years ago to 1770 C.E., as well as certain categories
of ethnological material dating from approximately
the second century B.C.E. to 1947 C.E, listed in the
Designated List, published as part of the final rule.
This follows the signing of the Cultural Property
Agreement (CPA) between India and US to prevent
and curb the illicit trafficking of antiquities from India
to the US.
Two Indian sculptures, which were previously in the
custody of the Smithsonian Museum in Washington
D.C.- Shiva and Uma (12th century), and Sundarar-
Parvati (16th century), are being repatriated to India.
Further, a Shiva Nataraja sculpture (9th century), which
was also in the custody of Smithsonian Museum, has
been loaned by Smithsonian’s National Museum of
Asian Art for a period of three years (2025-28).

Quad Engagement
Quad engagements at the Foreign Ministers’ level and
working-level continued to progress during the year.
Immediately after the new U.S. Administration took
office on 20 January, the Quad Foreign Ministers met in
person in Washington D.C. on 21 January, underlining
the value and importance of the Quad and its practical
initiatives aimed at addressing regional challenges in
the Indo-Pacific. A Joint Statement was released on
the occasion.
The Quad Foreign Ministers met for the second time in
the year in Washington, D.C. on 1 July and reiterated
their commitment to a free and open Indo-Pacific
region. With an aim to leverage the Quad’s resources
to address the region’s key challenges, the Ministers
announced a new, ambitious and strong Quad agenda
focused on four key areas - maritime and transnational
security, economic prosperity and security, critical and
emerging technology, and humanitarian assistance
and emergency response. They also launched the
Quad Critical Minerals Initiative, which aims to

text:
ANNUAL REPORT | 2025
238
strengthen economic security and collective resilience
by collaborating to secure and diversify critical
minerals supply chains. A Joint Statement and Joint
Factsheet were released following the meeting.
The Quad Foreign Ministers Meeting was held at the
Department of State in Washington D.C., July 2025.
A Quad Business Roundtable on Critical Minerals
was convened by the US Department of State
in Washington D.C. on 1 July to discuss shared
challenges and opportunities in securing reliable,
transparent and diversified critical minerals supply
chains. Senior representatives from companies and
business organisations from the Quad countries, as
well as officials from Quad embassies, participated in
the discussions.
In March, India hosted a Quad Workshop on Pandemic
Preparedness, with the participation of 15 Indo-Pacific
countries, to strengthen global health emergency
frameworks and enhance regional resilience.
Following the earthquake in Myanmar in March, Quad
countries released a Joint Statement highlighting their
coordinated response, including their contribution of
over USD 30 million in humanitarian assistance to
support affected communities.
With the objective of strengthening interoperability
and knowledge-sharing to address unlawful maritime
activities across the region, Quad partners undertook
the first-ever Quad-at-Sea Ship Observer Mission
from Palau to Guam, on 26 June –3 July, onboard US
Coast Guard Cutter Stratton.
The inaugural cohort of 18 students from Indo-Pacific
countries under the Quad STEM Scholarships Initiative,
announced by India during the 2024 Quad Leaders’
Summit, commenced their courses at renowned Indian
technical institutes in September 2025.
A Table Top Exercise under the Quad Indo-Pacific
Logistics Network (IPLN) was held in Hawaii on 28
April–2 May. The exercise simulated the leveraging of
Quad’s shared logistics capabilities in the Indo-Pacific
to support civilian response to natural disasters more
rapidly and efficiently across the region.
The inaugural Quad Ports of the Future Partnership
Conference was hosted by India in Mumbai on 29–
30 October, alongside India Maritime Week. The
Conference focused on leveraging Quad expertise to
support the development of sustainable and resilient
port infrastructure across the Indo-Pacific. Around
120 delegates from 24 countries, including the Quad
partners, participated in the Conference.
In October, under the Quad Advancing Innovation
to Empower NextGen Agriculture (AI-ENGAGE)
Initiative, India awarded grants to six joint research
proposals through the Indian Council of Agricultural
Research (ICAR), with the objective of leveraging
research and innovation in areas such as artificial
intelligence, robotics, communications, and sensing to
enhance crop yields and resilience.
The Annual Meeting and Table Top Exercise (TTX) of
the Quad Partnership on Humanitarian Assistance and
Disaster Relief (HADR) was held on 2–5 December in
Hawaii.
India hosted the third Quad Counter Terrorism
Working Group meeting and Table Top Exercise (TTX)
in New Delhi on 4–5 December.
The Quad Indo-Pacific Logistics Network Field
Training Exercise (FTX) was held in Guam from 8–12
December, on the sidelines of Operation Christmas
Drop at Andersen Air Force Base, Guam, with a focus

on enhancing interoperability and coordination among
Quad partners’ capabilities to better support regional

The next Quad Leaders’ Summit will be hosted by

Canada
India-Canada bilateral ties are underlined by shared
democratic values, a steadfast commitment to the rule
of law, vibrant people-to-people ties, robust economic
linkages and a strong commitment to upholding the
principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity.
On 29 April, in a post on X, the Prime Minister
conveyed congratulations to Prime Minister Mark
Carney on his election. This was reciprocated by
Prime Minister Mark Carney who called Prime
Minister on 6 June and extended him an invitation
to attend the G7 Summit in Kananaskis, held on 17
June. During the call, the two leaders acknowledged
the deep people-to-people ties between India and
Canada and reaffirmed their commitment to work
together with renewed vigour, guided by mutual
respect and shared interests.
High-Level Exchanges
Prime Minister visited Kananaskis, Canada on 16-
17 June to participate in the G7 outreach session
on ‘Energy Security: diversification, technology and
infrastructure to ensure access and affordability in a
changing world’. On the sidelines of the G7 Summit,
Prime Minister held a fruitful bilateral meeting with
Prime Minister Mark Carney. Both sides underlined
the need to pursue a constructive and balanced
partnership grounded in respect for mutual concerns
and sensitivities, strong people-to-people ties, and
growing economic complementarities. They also
agreed to take calibrated and constructive steps to
restore stability in the relationship, beginning with the
early return of High Commissioners to each other’s
capitals. Additionally, the two leaders underscored
the importance of restarting senior ministerial as
well as working level engagements across various
domains to rebuild trust and bring momentum to the
relationship.
On the sidelines of the G20 Leaders’ Summit in
Johannesburg, the Prime Minister held a bilateral
meeting with Prime Minister Carney on 23 November.
The leaders agreed to begin negotiations on a high-
ambition
Comprehensive
Economic
Partnership
Agreement (CEPA), aimed at doubling bilateral trade
to USD 50 billion by 2030. Prime Minister Carney
accepted Prime Minister’s invitation to visit India in
early 2026.
In Johannesburg, the Prime Ministers of India, Canada,
and Australia also launched the Australia–Canada–
India Technology and Innovation (ACITI) Partnership on
22 November. The initiative will foster cooperation on
critical and emerging technologies, with an emphasis
on artificial intelligence, green energy innovation, and
building resilient supply chains, including in critical
minerals.
Ministerial Engagements and Bilateral
Dialogues
EAM congratulated Anita Anand on her appointment
as Minister of Foreign Affairs of Canada on 13
May. Both foreign ministers also held a telephonic
conversation on 25 May. EAM and Canadian Foreign
Minister Anand also met on the sidelines of UNGA in
New York on 29 September.
Foreign Minister Anand visited India on 13-14
October. During her visit to New Delhi, she called
on the Prime Minister, held meetings with EAM
and the Minister of Commerce and Industry on 13
October. A joint statement – ‘Renewing Momentum
Towards a Stronger Partnership’ was issued by the
two foreign offices following the meeting between
the foreign ministers. The Ministers recognized that
in the context of ongoing global economic uncertainty
and rising geopolitical tensions, a strong and resilient
title: mea_annual_report

India-Canada bilateral relationship is essential. They
reaffirmed that reviving the partnership will help create
opportunities for enhanced economic cooperation,
mitigate vulnerabilities arising from shifting global
alliances, ensure more reliable supply chains, and
reinforce strategic stability in an increasingly complex
international environment. Both sides agreed to
work on a New Roadmap for India-Canada bilateral
relations. During the Mumbai leg of her visit, Foreign
Minister Anand met the Chief Minister of Maharashtra.
In Mumbai, Minister Anand also engaged with senior
leaders of India’s top corporations, highlighting
Canada as a premier destination for investment
and collaboration in areas such as clean energy,
infrastructure, technology, and innovation. In addition,
she met Canadian pension fund and institutional
investors based in Mumbai, recognising their critical
role in strengthening Canada–India economic linkages
and mobilising capital for sustainable growth.
At the invitation of Foreign Minister Anand, EAM
visited Canada to participate in Day-two of the Second
2025 G7 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting held in Niagara
Region, Ontario on 11-12 November.
EAM and Foreign Minister of Canada Anita Anand on the

for rebuilding trust and strengthening, expanding
and reinforcing existing mechanisms of engagement
between respective law enforcement agencies.
Both sides also discussed advancing cooperation
in intelligence exchanges, countering terrorism and

a telephonic conversation with the Minister of

beneficial opportunities for Indian and Canadian

offered by the two economies.
At the invitation of CIM, Minister Sidhu, undertook an
official visit to India on 11–14 November. The Ministers
held the seventh edition of the Ministerial Dialogue on
Trade and Investment (MDTI) on 13 November in New
Delhi. During the visit, Minister Sidhu also met the
Minister of Petroleum and Natural Gas and discussed
bilateral trade and investment opportunities in the

Trade and Economic Cooperation
Trade and investment linkages remain central pillars of
the India–Canada bilateral partnership. India’s exports
to Canada during January–December stood at USD
4.485 billion, registering a growth of 8.28 percent.
India’s imports from Canada during the same period
amounted to USD 3.339 billion, reflecting a decline of
30.97 percent. Total bilateral trade during the period
was USD 7.824 billion, representing a year-on-year
contraction of 12.87 percent.
During the meeting between the Foreign Ministers of
the two countries in New Delhi on 13 October, both
sides affirmed that trade is the cornerstone of bilateral
economic growth and resilience, and acknowledged
the expanding opportunities in goods, services,
and investment. They agreed that early initiatives in
trade cooperation would include commencing, at an
early date, ministerial-level discussions on bilateral
trade and investment, informed by current economic
realities and respective strategic priorities. Both sides
also agreed to resume the Canada–India CEO Forum,
which will bring together leading business executives
from both countries to identify concrete and actionable
recommendations to facilitate enhanced bilateral trade
and investment, with a focus on priority sectors such
as clean technology, infrastructure, agri-food, and
digital innovation. The Forum is expected to convene
on the margins of a senior-level trade mission in early
2026.
During the visit of Canada’s Minister of International
Trade Maninder Sidhu to India, the two sides held the
seventh Ministerial Dialogue on Trade and Investment
(MDTI) in New Delhi on 13 November. CIM and Minister
Sidhu reaffirmed the strength and continuity of the
India–Canada economic partnership and reiterated
their commitment to deepening cooperation through
sustained dialogue, mutual respect, and forward-
looking initiatives. They welcomed the robust growth
in bilateral trade in goods and services, as well as
the steady expansion of two-way investment flows,
and reaffirmed their shared commitment to elevating
the economic partnership in line with evolving global
trade and supply chain dynamics.
While in New Delhi, Minister Sidhu held high-level
meetings with leading Indian companies, including
Bhartia Group, Tata Group, and HCL Technologies,
and participated in a roundtable with representatives
of Canadian pension funds, Air Canada, and other
Canadian companies to explore new avenues for

Portfolio investments from Canada into India currently
exceed USD 75 billion and are expected to grow
further, reflecting confidence in India’s long-term
economic prospects. Canadian FDI in India between
April 2000 and June 2025 amounted to USD
4.18 billion. Over 600 Canadian companies have
established a presence in India, while nearly 1,000
Canadian companies are actively pursuing business

Energy and Climate Cooperation
Recognising the pivotal role of energy transformation
in meeting climate goals, enhancing energy security,
and supporting sustainable economic development,
India and Canada intend to deepen cooperation in
clean, secure, and equitable energy collaboration.
Both sides have committed to revitalise the energy
partnership through the early re-establishment of the
Canada–India Ministerial Energy Dialogue (CIMED)
and its accompanying Action Plan. Canada’s Minister
of Natural Resources Tim Hodgson, accepted the
invitation of Minister of Petroleum and Natural Gas
to participate in India Energy Week, scheduled to
be held in Goa from 27–30 January 2026. The two
sides aim to promote two-way trade in LNG and
LPG and encourage investments in oil and gas
exploration and production, with a strong emphasis
on clean technologies. Cooperation will also extend
to sustainable low-carbon fuels and technologies,
including green hydrogen, biofuels, carbon capture,
utilisation and storage (CCUS), and electric mobility,
alongside efforts to strengthen related supply chains,
policy frameworks, and market access.
India and Canada will exchange best practices in
electricity system management to enhance grid safety,
stability, and the integration of renewable energy
sources. Joint efforts will also focus on emissions
reduction, environmental management, digitalisation
of the power sector, and disaster resilience. Both
countries will continue to advance global energy
efficiency initiatives, including through multilateral
platforms such as the G20.
Recognising Canada’s strengths in the mining
sector, both sides will also facilitate dialogue among
governments, industry, and think tanks to explore
how Canadian mining expertise can support India’s
critical minerals requirements for energy security. The
two countries also welcomed ongoing discussions on
civil nuclear cooperation as part of their broader clean
energy transition agenda, including engagements
between India’s Department of Atomic Energy and
Canadian uranium suppliers on existing and potential
new mining projects. To strengthen collaboration in
this area, India and Canada have agreed to convene
the Critical Minerals Annual Dialogue.
A delegation of senior officials from Ministry Mines,
NALCO, Coal India, GSI, NMDC and UCIL participated
in the Premier Mineral Exploration & Mining Convention
(PDAC) – the world’s premier mineral exploration and
mining convention held in Toronto on 2-5 March.
Technology Cooperation
Recognising the pivotal role of innovation and
technology in advancing inclusive growth and
global competitiveness, India and Canada agreed to
strengthen their partnership in addressing climate
challenges through science, technology, and digital

Canada’s Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital
Innovation Evan Solomon accepted the invitation of the
Minister of Electronics and Information Technology to
attend the India AI Impact Summit held in New Delhi
on 19–20 February 2026. The Summit is expected to
serve as a platform to exchange ideas on AI-driven
solutions for clean energy, climate adaptation, and
environmental sustainability. Canada is also officiating
as the Co-Chair of the Working Group on Science for
the AI Impact Summit to take place in New Delhi. The
Working Group on Science envisions a world where
AI accelerates discovery through open, transparent,
and equitable scientific collaboration bridging divides
in capacity and participation. It aims to build collective
understanding and shared norms to ensure that AI
enhances, rather than narrows, the frontiers of global
science.
Both sides will also explore cooperation in digital

effective climate action, transparent governance, and
sustainable growth.
Agriculture Cooperation
Recognising
the

collaboration in agriculture to promote food security,
enhance trade and productivity, increase farmers’
incomes, and ensure long-term sectoral sustainability,
India and Canada agreed to work together to build
stable and sustainable supply chains. Cooperation
will focus on improving agri-value chains through
the exchange of best practices and technological
collaboration, while enhancing nutritional security
and promoting the recycling of agricultural waste
into energy and organic fertilisers. The partnership
will also emphasise innovation in climate-resilient
agriculture and sustainable food systems, supporting
shared objectives of environmental stewardship,
economic opportunity, and resilient rural livelihoods.
FICCI led a delegation to Saskatchewan’s premier
agricultural technology exhibition ‘Ag in Motion’ on
14-18 July. The 21-member delegation included
officials from Department of Agriculture & Farmers’
Welfare, Maharashtra’s Indo Pulses Development
Association, and Punjab Chamber of Commerce.
During September–October, the Canadian province
of Saskatchewan organised the Saskatchewan Trade
and Investment Roadshow (STAIR), focused on
agriculture and agri-technology, across four Indian
cities—Hyderabad, Kolkata, Mumbai, and Lucknow.
Education Cooperation
Canada has emerged as a favoured destination for
Indian students, with the current number estimated
at approximately 392,810. Both sides agreed to
pursue renewed collaboration in higher education
and research, reflecting the expanding talent pools
and innovation ecosystems in both countries.
Emphasis will be placed on research partnerships in
emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence,
cybersecurity, and fintech, alongside efforts to expand
the presence of Canadian academic institutions in India
through overseas campuses. To advance these goals,
both sides will revitalise the Joint Working Group
on Higher Education, providing renewed impetus to
India–Canada academic networks and institutional
linkages, and further strengthening the people-to-
people foundation of the bilateral relationship.
People-to-People Exchanges
People-to-people linkages form the cornerstone of
mutual understanding and long-term collaboration
between India and Canada. Canada hosts one of the
largest Indian diasporas abroad, comprising nearly
1.8 million Indo-Canadians and approximately one
million non-resident Indians. The diaspora, primarily
concentrated in the Greater Toronto Area, Greater
Vancouver Area, Montreal (Quebec), Calgary and
Edmonton (Alberta), Ottawa (Ontario), and Winnipeg
(Manitoba), has contributed significantly to Canadian
society and the economy. Numerous business and
diaspora organisations continue to support enhanced

diverse engagements between the countries.

The Prime Minister paid a historic visit to Argentina on

Javier Milei. The two leaders called for enhancing

India’s engagement with Chile intensified in 2025
with high level political engagement and strong focus
on expansion of trade and economic ties. The two
countries have continued to coordinate their positions
at multilateral fora in support of multilateralism,
sustainable development and promotion of human
rights. Chile has reiterated its support for India’s claim
to permanent membership of UNSC.
President of Chile Gabriel Boric’s State Visit to India
in April was a watershed moment in the bilateral
relations, which infused new energy in the relationship
and paved the way for enhanced engagement across
sectors. During the visit, the two countries decided to
launch negotiations for a Comprehensive Economic
Partnership Agreement. Since then, four rounds of
negotiations have already taken place. The visit also
resulted in the signing of documents for cooperation
in disaster management, mineral resources, Antarctica
and cultural exchange program.

during his State Visit to India, April 2025.

in the 10th CII India-Latin America Conclave. She
again visited India in December to participate in the
fourth round of CEPA negotiations. During these two
visits she met the Minister of Commerce and Industry
and discussed opportunities for increasing trade and
economic relations between the two countries.

delegation visited Chile to participate in the Summit
meeting at the Congreso Futuro and the third World
Summit of the Committees of the Future in Santiago.

innovations, technologies, culture and education. The

Machine Learning, digital innovation and emerging

text:
ANNUAL REPORT | 2025
250
An All-Party Parliamentary Delegation, led by a
senior Member of the Lok Sabha paid an official visit to
Colombia on 29-31 May. The purpose of the visit was
to convey India’s firm and resolute commitment to
combating terrorism in all its forms and manifestations.
The delegation interacted with senior officials from
Colombia including Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs
Rosa Yolanda Villavicencio, various parliamentarians,
journalists and media representatives, among others.
The delegation conveyed India’s zero-tolerance policy
towards terrorism and its proactive approach to
addressing cross-border threats.
Secretary (East) paid an official visit to Colombia on
21-22 August. During the visit, he held meetings
with the Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs, Ministers of
Culture, Information & Communications Technology
and Vice Minister of Commerce, Industry, and Tourism.
The meetings underscored the shared commitment of
both the countries to deepen political and economic
cooperation, and enhance partnerships in innovation,
technology, and people-to-people ties.
India was announced as the Guest of Honour Country
for the 2026 Bogota International Book Fair (FILBo) on
5 August, marking an important milestone in cultural
and literary exchange between India and Colombia.
In December, as part of India’s global outreach on
counter-terrorism, the exhibition ‘Human Cost of
Terrorism’, was organized at the Gabriel García
Márquez Cultural Center in Bogota on 9-15 December.
Bilateral trade for the period January – October stood
at approximately USD 3.8 billion, with imports from
Colombia at USD 2.4 billion and exports to Colombia
of USD 1.4 billion. Various Export Promotion Councils
such as The Cotton Textiles Export Promotion Council
(TEXPROCIL), Manmade and Technical Textiles
Export Promotion Council (MATEXIL), Services Export
Promotion Council (SEPC), Trade Promotion Council
of India (TPCI), led Indian delegations to Colombia
during the year, providing further impetus to the
bilateral trade relations. It is expected that a CEPA will
be concluded between the two countries at an early
date to further provide impetus to bilateral trade.
Ecuador
This year, Ecuador and India commemorated 56
years of diplomatic relations, marking an important
milestone in their long-standing friendship. Bilateral
trade for the period January - October stood at
approximately USD 464 million, with imports from
Ecuador at USD 126 million and exports to Ecuador
of USD 338 million.
MoS (PM) visited Ecuador on 4-5 November. During
his visit, he called on President of the Republic of

251
Ecuador Daniel Noboa Azin, met Foreign Minister
Gabriela Sommerfeld, and other Ministers/Vice-
Ministers.
The year also marked a significant upgrade in India’s
diplomatic engagement with Ecuador, with the
opening of a resident Mission in Quito. MoS (PM) jointly
inaugurated the Embassy with the Foreign Minister
of Ecuador Gabriela Sommerfeld on 5 November in
Quito. This development upgraded India's diplomatic
presence from concurrent accreditation (previously
handled by the Embassy in Bogota, Colombia) to
a full-fledged resident Mission, reflecting India's
commitment to deepening engagement with Latin
America and the Global South.
In August, the ‘Gandhi and Sacred India’ exhibition
was inaugurated in Cuenca by the Ambassador of
India to Ecuador, alongside the city’s Mayor Cristian
Zamora, celebrating India’s moral and spiritual legacy
and deepening cultural cooperation with Ecuadorian
academic and municipal institutions.
Guyana
Prime Minister of Guyana Brig (Ret'd) Mark Anthony
Phillips visited India on 4-7 March to attend World
Sustainable Development Summit. First Lady of
Guyana Arya Ali visited India to attend the Kumbh
Global Summit on Development and Sustainability
in February. Minister of Health Frank Anthony visited
India to attend International Health Dialogue on 21-
22 February.
A five-member delegation led by the Permanent
Secretary of Home Affairs of Guyana visited India on
13-18 April to attend the All-India Forensic Science
Conference in New Delhi. A two-member team
from National Forensics Science University (NFSU)
visited Guyana on 23-26 June, and discussed the
establishment of Forensic center in Guyana.
Taking the India-Guyana development partnership
forward, an important road connectivity project, ‘East
Bank-East Coast Road Linkage Project’, completed
under LoC of USD 50 million was inaugurated on 1
July.
A team from ISRO participated in the Global
Biodiversity Alliance Summit hosted by Guyana. The
ISRO team focused on promoting space applications
for sustainable development, biodiversity, disaster risk
reduction and climate studies. It opens a new chapter
in our growing multifaceted ties.
Paraguay
President of Paraguay Santiago Peña Palacios paid
a State Visit to India on 2-4 June. President Peña
was accompanied by the senior Ministers, members
of Parliament, the Governor, and other senior
officials. Prime Minister and President Peña held a
comprehensive discussion on the entire spectrum of
bilateral relations, including trade and investment,
health and pharmaceuticals, defence and security,
infrastructure,
mining
and
mineral
resources,
agriculture and food security, green energy, ICTs,
digitalisation,
innovation,
disaster
management,
science and technology, education and links between
peoples. Both sides signed the agreement for the
establishment of the Joint Commission Mechanism
(JCM) at the level of Vice ministers. The JCM will
serve as an important platform to review and explore
collaboration in various sectors of common interest.
Both sides also agreed to work together for expanding
existing trade links under the India-MERCOSUR
Preferential Trade Agreement (PTA).
Prime Minister held a bilateral meeting with President of
Paraguay Santiago Peña Palacios during his State Visit to
India, June 2025.

ANNUAL REPORT | 2025
252
Under the India–UN Development Partnership Fund,
two key projects have been successfully completed
in Paraguay. The first project, titled ‘Prevention of
Teenage Pregnancy and Violence/Sexual Abuse in
Girls and Adolescents from an Intersectoral Approach’
was completed in 2022 with a total value of USD 1
million. The project focussed on improving adolescent
health and protecting young girls from violence and
abuse. The second project, titled – ‘Maternal and Child
Health care’ was completed in 2025 with a value of
USD 1.49 million.
The Chamber of Senators of Paraguay’s National
Congress
established
the
Paraguay-India
Parliamentary Friendship Commission in October. The
first meeting of India-Paraguay JCM took place on 14
November in Asuncion. It was co-chaired by Secretary
(East) and Vice-Minister of Foreign Affairs of Paraguay
Victor Verdun.
A High-Level Closing Event for the India-UN
Development Partnership Fund USD 1.49 million
project ‘Extension of Access and Coverage in
Maternal and Child Health in Remote Rural Areas,
Indigenous Communities, and Border Areas of the
Paraguayan Chaco’ was held on 15 November in
Asuncion. Secretary (East) participated as Guest of
Honor and delivered the Keynote Address. Paraguay
became member of Coalition for Disaster Resilient
Infrastructure (CDRI) in December.
A delegation from RITES visited Paraguay in July to
discuss rejuvenation of Railway Sector in Paraguay at
the invitation of Paraguayan side.
Peru
This was a pivotal year for India-Peru relations, marked
by many high-level exchanges held during important
events. The then Foreign Minister of Peru Elmer
Schialer visited India on 16-20 March to participate in
the Raisina Dialogue 2025. He also met EAM on the
sidelines of the Dialogue, and discussed progress in
bilateral/multilateral relations.
Minister of Foreign Trade and Tourism of Peru Ursula
León visited India on 18-21 March and participated
in the 10th CII India LAC Business conclave. During
the visit, Minister León met Minister of Commerce and
Industries and Minister of Culture & Tourism.
Secretary (East) and Joint Secretary (South America)
visited Perú on 23-26 August. Secretary (East) met
Vice Foreign Minister, Minister of Health and Vice
Minister of Defence Resources during the visit.
Secretary (Agriculture) led five-member delegation
to Peru on 1-6 June. The delegation visited the
International Potato Center (CIP), Lima and interacted
with the then Agriculture Minister of Peru Angel
Manero, Rector of National Agricultural University.
EAM met the then Foreign Minister of Peru Elmer Schialer on
the sidelines of the Raisina Dialogue, March 2025.
A Rajya Sabha-member led the Indian delegation
for 11th Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU) Global
Conference of Young Parliamentarians for Gender
Equality, held at Lima on 11-13 September.
A 25-member Indian mining sector delegation
led by Joint Secretary (Mines), participated in the
biennial Mining Conclave PeruMin’25, held on 22-26
September. The Indian & Peruvian Mining Ministries
also held the fourth meeting of Joint Working Group
on Mining to further strengthen bilateral cooperation,
on the sidelines of PeruMin’25.
India donated 2,50,000 bottles (100ml) of saline
solution to Peru, upon the latter’s request to tide over a
health emergency. The consignment has reached Peru
on 24 October and was handed over to the Peruvian
side in a formal function on 12 December.
Indian Mission, Lima with Indian Association of Peru
(IAP) celebrated Diwali and also donated funds

Peru continues to be among the top five trading
partners of India in Latin America. India is the third
largest trading partner, 11th largest source of imports
and 3rd largest export destination for Peru. The trade
between India and Peru during the Financial Year
2024-25 totaled USD 5.912 billion, of which India’s
exports were worth USD 1.002 billion and imports
from Peru were USD 4.91 billion. The eighth round of
negotiations for the India-Peru Free Trade Agreement
(FTA) was conducted virtually in August and the ninth
round took place in Lima on 3-5 November 2025.

Saint Kitts and Nevis opened its Resident Mission
in May, opening a new chapter in bilateral relations.
Minister of Public Infrastructure, Energy and Utilities,
Domestic Transport, Information, Communication
and Technology, and Post Konris G. Maynard visited
India on 27-30 October to attend the eighth General
International Solar Alliance Assembly held in New
Delhi.
A scoping team visited St. Kitts & Nevis on 30-

Development Partnership Administration programme
of MEA, before supplying SME machinery and
equipment under the USD 1 million SME Grant project
extended to CARICOM nations.

on 7 July, on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit, held
in Rio de Janeiro. The leaders discussed deepening of
bilateral relationship in areas such as trade, chemicals,
pharmaceuticals, technology, and defence, among
others. Prime Minister also conveyed India’s decision
to open a resident Mission in Montevideo.

Partnership Fund for the project, ‘Support for Social

strengthened across several areas and marked by
strong cooperation at regional and multilateral fora
such as CARICOM (Caribbean Community), SICA
(Central American Integration System) and CELAC
(Community of Latin American and Caribbean States).
The increased political engagements during 2025
provided a renewed momentum to the relationships.
Prime Minister paid a state visit to Trinidad and
Tobago on 3-4 July, highlighting the importance the

Cuba Miguel Diaz-Canel Bermudez in July.

by the EAM from Indian side and Minister of Foreign
Affairs of the Republic of Panama Javier Martínez-
Acha, in his capacity as Pro Tempore Presidency of
SICA.

session of the UNGA in New York, September 2025.
